summary: This informational document describes the plan to move responsibility for bridging-related MIB modules from the IETF Bridge MIB Working Group to the IEEE 802.1 Working Group, which develops the bridging technology those MIBs manage.

eli5.summary: The people who make the rules for network bridges moved the job of writing their monitoring lists to the group that already designs the bridges themselves.

questions: why did bridge mib work move to ieee 802.1
subtitle: The plan for handing bridge MIB modules from an IETF working group to the IEEE group that designs bridges.

tldr.problem: The bridging MIB modules were maintained by the IETF Bridge MIB WG, while the technology they manage is developed by the IEEE 802.1 WG, and the IETF Bridge MIB WG did not intend to develop MIB modules in the future.
tldr.mechanism: Future MIB work moves to IEEE 802.1, the existing IETF modules are frozen in place, authors' permissions are sought, and IETF MIB Doctors offer loose, optional review of IEEE modules.
tldr.outcome: It sets expectations between the two organizations and keeps existing IETF documents valid and unchanged for backward compatibility.

today: RFC 4663 is Informational, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the 2006 plan to move bridge MIB work to IEEE 802.1 and does not say what later happened.

sections.title: The Transition Plan
sections.content:
RFC 4663 describes the plan to move responsibility for bridging-related MIB modules from the IETF Bridge MIB Working Group to the IEEE 802.1 Working Group. A MIB module defines objects used to manage a technology, usually through SNMP. The modules in question are the documents RFC 4188, RFC 4318, RFC 4363 and RFC 1525.

The aim is clear expectations between the IETF and IEEE so that the IESG, IAB, IETF and IEEE can review the plan. Case-by-case situations are left to the liaisons.
sections.eli5: Two clubs share a job. This note says which club does it from now on and how they will help each other.

sections.title: Why Move the Work
sections.content:
The 802.1 community needs SNMP MIB modules for its technologies, so it should charter that work in each new project's Project Authorization Request (PAR), and include it in maintenance projects. The IESG has required IETF working groups that produce a protocol to also develop its MIB module, partly to get the content experts involved in the management design.

The IETF encourages other standards bodies to bring subject matter expertise or, better, to take the lead themselves. It finds it acceptable for IEEE 802 to write MIB documents, and offers help reviewing them from an SNMP, MIB and SMI perspective, even after the transition.
sections.eli5: The people who know how bridges work are best placed to write down how to watch them, so the job goes to them.

sections.title: Handing Over the Documents
sections.content:
For new work, the latest 802.1 PARs, starting with P802.1ah approved in December 2004, include explicit text on SNMP management. Submitters of new bridge-management work should be directed to the 802.1 WG and advised not to publish their MIB modules as Internet-Drafts. The RFC stresses publishing MIB modules in ASCII format, because most network management systems can import ASCII but not PDF. IEEE 802 specifications are available for a fee for the first six months after approval, and free afterward.

On object identifiers, IETF and IEEE 802 have separate registration branches. The RFC does not recommend adding a few objects to the IANA-controlled tree, because of coordination difficulties. It prefers an IEEE MIB module with a new compliance clause, and keeping existing trees in place to minimize disruption.

For existing documents, the IETF lacks the legal authority to transfer them without the authors' consent, so the 802.1 WG needs permission from the authors or their companies, using a sample letter in Appendix B. Items deferred to the IEEE include the autoEdgePort parameter and the BridgeID object. The plan is that the current Bridge MIB modules are "frozen in time" and updated only through independent MIB modules written by 802.1. The Bridge MIB WG has completed its documents and been closed.
sections.eli5: New lists will be written by the bridge people. The old lists are kept exactly as they are so nothing breaks, but the bridge people ask the original writers' permission before copying them.

sections.title: MIB Doctor Reviews of IEEE Modules
sections.content:
IETF MIB Doctors are expert reviewers of MIB modules. The RFC describes a loose offering: the IETF keeps a group that can review IEEE 802 MIB modules when a MIB Doctor is available and willing. Whether to take the advice is up to the 802.1 editors and chairs. It suggests requesting a review early, after the design is set, and again only for important ballots. It also recommends that 802.1 set up its own MIB Doctor team, which the IETF is willing to help train.

Reviewers should use the guidelines in RFC 4181, with listed exceptions: the IANA and copyright sections do not apply as written, and the naming hierarchy follows the 802.1 OID root. For global problems, MIB Doctors need not supply replacement text for each instance. A review inside 802.1 is more like a working group chair asking for a sanity check than a formal IETF review, so the RFC warns against implying that IEEE documents received a formal MIB Doctor review.
sections.eli5: Experienced checkers from one club offer to look over the other club's work if they have time, like a friend proofreading your essay, but it is not an official grade.

sections.title: Intellectual Property Conclusions
sections.content:
Teleconferences on November 29, 2005 and January 11, 2006 reviewed the legal side. The IETF and ISOC receive a non-exclusive copyright license from RFC authors, and the authors keep their other rights. Anyone can reproduce an RFC as-is. If the authors give another group permission to create derivative works, that agreement is between the authors and that group, so no ISOC copyright notice is needed on the new document, and the IETF cannot require a pointer to the RFC.

The IETF still keeps its own permission to make derivatives within its standards process. It strongly recommends that other bodies acknowledge the RFCs a work derives from, and notes that MIB modules following RFC 4181 contain REVISION clauses recording where earlier versions were published.
sections.eli5: Writers lend their work to the IETF, but they can also let another group copy and change it. The IETF asks that group to say where the idea came from.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC describes a plan to move MIB module responsibility and says it does not impact security. It discusses IANA assignment of object identifiers, but no IANA actions are required.
sections.eli5: This is only a plan about who does the work, so it does not change how safe anything is.
